records.sourceFile: Two periodization strategies in professional football and their influence on accumulated training load and its distribution - Differences between starters and non-starters.pdf

paper.citation: Marín K, Castellano J. Two periodization strategies in professional football and their influence on accumulated training load and its distribution: Differences between starters and non-starters. J Sports Sci. 2024.
paper.abstract: Compared weekly training load, training monotony and training strain in 80 professional football players, using GPS. Two microcycle lengths (6 and 7 days between matches) and two post-match periodization strategies (compensatory session on MD+1 or MD+2) were analysed separately for starters and non-starters.
paper.tldr: Non-starters carried more training load than starters in most weekly measures, and the timing of the post-match session changed how load was shared. Plan load separately by playing status, session timing and microcycle length.
paper.methods: Four seasons of GPS data (10 Hz) from training sessions only; match-day data were excluded. Variables were total distance, Player Load, high-speed and sprint distance, accelerations and decelerations, with monotony and strain derived from them. Groups were compared with Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests with Cohen's d effect sizes.
paper.findings: Non-starters accumulated higher training load than starters in most variables in both microcycle lengths. Non-starters accumulated more under P1 than under P2, with moderate to large effects in high-speed and sprint distance, Player Load and total distance, while starters had higher values for some load, monotony and strain variables under P2 than under P1 (trivial to moderate effects). The 7-day week produced higher load for both groups, and the locomotor variables in the 7-day P2 week were the exception to the non-starter pattern.
paper.limitations: Observational design from a single club. Competition load was excluded by design, and heart rate, perceived exertion and wellness data were not included. The paper notes that congested schedules and travel were not modelled.
paper.practicalImplications: Set the compensatory session by playing status. Where it cannot fall on match day, train non-starters on MD+1 to keep the stimulus close to competition. Use MD+2 to give starters more load when they can take it. Check monotony and strain when moving between 3- and 4-session weeks.
paper.athleteDev: Use the load comparison to set compensatory sessions for non-starters and recovery sessions for starters, and check monotony and strain when microcycle length changes.
paper.rtp: The study covers healthy squad players only and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Type 1 Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy after Blood Flow–restricted Training in Powerlifters.pdf

paper.citation: Bjørnsen T, Wernbom M, Kirketeig A, Paulsen G, Samnøy L, Bækken L, et al. Type 1 Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy after Blood Flow-restricted Training in Powerlifters. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(2):288-298.
paper.abstract: Seventeen national-level powerlifters were randomised to two 1-week blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted front squats or conventional heavy front squat training within a 6.5-week programme. Muscle biopsies, ultrasound measures and strength tests were taken before and after the programme.
paper.tldr: Two short blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted squats added to a strength programme produced more type I fibre growth and quadriceps size than heavy squats in elite powerlifters, but not more maximal strength. For strength-focused athletes this is a muscle-size finding only.
paper.methods: Randomised controlled trial in 17 national-level powerlifters. The BFRRE group performed four front squat sets at about 30% of 1RM with thigh pressure of about 120 mm Hg in weeks 1 and 3; the control group performed heavy front squats at 60-85% of 1RM. Outcomes were muscle fibre area, myonuclei, satellite cells, ultrasound muscle size, isokinetic knee extension torque and front squat 1RM.
paper.findings: The BFRRE group had larger increases in type I fibre area (12% vs 0%) and type I myonuclei (18% vs 0%), and larger vastus lateralis cross-sectional area (7.7% vs 0.5%, P=0.04). Knee extension torque increased only in the BFRRE group (P=0.04) and 1RM increased only in the control group (P=0.02); no between-group strength difference was found. Satellite cell counts did not change.
paper.limitations: Small groups and a short intervention, with limited power for type II fibre effects. Cuff pressure was set with elastic wraps, and the strength test was front squat, a lift the powerlifters were less practised in.
paper.practicalImplications: Short blocks of low-load blood flow-restricted squats can add quadriceps size without heavy loads, but this trial does not support expecting a maximal strength gain from them. Keep high-load training in the programme.
paper.athleteDev: Consider short low-load blood flow-restricted squat blocks alongside heavy training when muscle size is the goal; the trial showed no strength advantage over heavy front squats.
paper.rtp: The trial enrolled healthy elite athletes and included no injury or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Understanding the Science of Resistance Training- An Evolutionary Perspective.pdf

paper.citation: Kraemer WJ, Ratamess NA, Flanagan SD, Shurley JP, Todd JS, Todd TC. Understanding the Science of Resistance Training: An Evolutionary Perspective. Sports Med. 2017.
paper.abstract: The history of resistance training research began with anecdotal ideas and grew slowly from the late 1890s through the 1970s. The mid-1970s marked a shift from strength assessment toward physiological systems, physical health and performance. Direct citation analysis identified ten major research areas.
paper.tldr: Resistance training research grew from practitioner anecdote into a multi-branch science. For staff, it is useful background on where current RT evidence came from.
paper.methods: Brief narrative historical review with no described search for the historical sections. A bibliometric analysis searched the Web of Science Core Collection with RT key terms (12,117 hits, refined to 7858 articles and 458 reviews) and used co-citation, co-occurrence and direct citation network analysis in VOSviewer and CitNetExplorer.
paper.findings: The authors describe the evolution of RT research from early strength testing and practitioner-led work, through the 1940s to 1970s studies of DeLorme's progressive resistance exercise and the muscle fiber and neural work of the 1970s and 1980s, to branches covering physiology, nutrition, biomechanics, recovery, injury prevention and rehabilitation. The bibliometric analysis found steady growth since 2000 (average yearly publication growth of 11%) and ten citation communities, the largest focused on the physical consequences of RE (n = 4743) and on cellular, molecular and physiological aspects (n = 4314).
paper.limitations: The historical review is selective by design and has no quantitative synthesis. The bibliometric search used one database and measures citation links, which reflect influence rather than evidence quality, and its historical framing is not a current evidence grade.
paper.practicalImplications: Use it as context for why current RT programming rests on decades of mixed practitioner and laboratory work. It does not provide a program to copy.
paper.athleteDev: Shows that the strength and power training methods used in athlete programs, such as repetition-maximum loading and multi-set programming, were built from a long line of studies. It does not itself test any training program.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation decisions for injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: Velocity loss as a critical variable determing the adaptations to strength training.pdf

paper.citation: Pareja-Blanco F, Alcazar J, Sánchez-Valdepeñas J, Cornejo-Daza PJ, Piqueras-Sanchiz F, Mora-Vela R, et al. Velocity Loss as a Critical Variable Determining the Adaptations to Strength Training. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020;52(8):1752-1762.
paper.abstract: The study compared four 8-week resistance training programmes with velocity loss thresholds of 0%, 10%, 20% and 40% in each set, using the full squat. Outcomes included muscle hypertrophy and architecture, tensiomyography, sprint, jump, isometric strength, a progressive loading test and fatigue. No between-group differences were found for sprint, jump or strength gains despite different total volumes. Higher thresholds (20% and 40%) maximised hypertrophy, but the 40% threshold also produced negative neuromuscular changes.
paper.tldr: Only the 20% and 40% velocity loss groups showed significant within-group muscle growth, although the between-group difference was not significant (P = 0.06), and the 40% group also worsened on some neuromuscular measures. Strength and jump gains were similar across thresholds, so moderate thresholds look like the sensible middle ground.
paper.methods: Sixty-four resistance-trained men were randomised to VL0, VL10, VL20 or VL40 groups, training the full squat for 8 weeks with three sets at 70-85% 1RM. Hypertrophy, architecture, tensiomyography, sprint, jump, strength and fatigue were tested before and after training. Nine participants dropped out, so all outcomes are reported for 55 men; there was no non-training control group.
paper.findings: No between-group differences in sprint, jump or strength gains. VL20 and VL40 showed significant within-group increases in muscle hypertrophy (P < 0.001), but the group-time interaction was P = 0.06. Only VL40 showed a slower delay time in the vastus lateralis (group-time interaction P = 0.05) and a decrease in early rate of force development (P = 0.04).
paper.limitations: Only one exercise and one 8-week programme were studied, in men who were resistance-trained and physically active rather than sport-specific athletes, with no control group and no control of energy or protein intake. The hypertrophy group interaction was not significant at P < 0.05, and the authors caution that rate of force development measures had poor reliability (CV 12.8% to 24.3%).
paper.practicalImplications: Moderate velocity loss thresholds appear to balance strength and muscle gains against negative neuromuscular effects in this population. Very high thresholds such as 40% may add fatigue-related neuromuscular costs without extra strength gain.
paper.athleteDev: For squat-based strength blocks, set a moderate velocity loss threshold rather than training to near-failure every set. In this sample, strength and jump gains were similar across thresholds, while sprint times barely changed in any group.
paper.rtp: The study was in healthy resistance-trained men and did not test injured athletes. It cannot be used to guide return-to-sport loading decisions.

records.sourceFile: Virtual training, real effects - A narrative review on sports performance enhancement through interventions in virtual reality.pdf

paper.citation: Richlan F, Weiß M, Kastner P, Braid J. Virtual training, real effects: a narrative review on sports performance enhancement through interventions in virtual reality. Front Psychol. 2023;14:1240790.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of 12 pre-post VR intervention studies across many sports, with aggregate N=493 novice, amateur and expert athletes, showing often significant gains in target skills.
paper.tldr: VR training has produced real skill gains in several sports, often beating passive or conventional training. Transfer to competition is still an open question.
paper.methods: Literature search of Web of Science, Google Scholar and PubMed, last searched July 4, 2022. Of 51 preselected articles, 12 peer-reviewed pre-post intervention studies met inclusion criteria. Study design, sport, VR technology and outcomes were extracted for a narrative summary.
paper.findings: Included studies covered archery, bowling, curling, darts, golf, baseball, table tennis, soccer, basketball, karate, cycling and balance tasks. Many reported statistically significant effects on target skills after VR training, often outperforming passive or active control conditions, although in expert golfers a VR warm-up was followed by a significant drop in performance on the first real putt. The review also discusses neurocognitive mechanisms such as visual search and imagery.
paper.limitations: Only 12 studies were included, and they differ in sport, skill level, VR system and outcome. Real-world transfer and generalizability are discussed as unresolved.
paper.practicalImplications: VR training may add useful practice for perceptual-cognitive, decision-making and imagery skills in some sports. The authors conclude that general recommendations for or against VR in applied practice are premature, so use should be tied to a specific skill and checked locally.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: VR can supplement training of visual search, decision-making and imagery, and one baseball study found larger gains when difficulty was adapted to the batter. Evidence of transfer to competition comes from a few small studies, such as higher next-season on-base percentage after adaptive VR batting practice.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Most included samples were healthy; one study in university soccer players with chronic low back pain reported larger pain and wellness improvements after screen-based VR training than after isokinetic or conventional training. The review does not evaluate return to sport and should not be used for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: What we do not know about stretching in healthy athletes - A scoping review with evidence gap map from 200 trials.pdf

paper.citation: Afonso J, Andrade R, Rocha-Rodrigues S, Nakamura FY, Sarmento H, Freitas SR, et al. What We Do Not Know About Stretching in Healthy Athletes: A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map from 300 Trials. Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: This systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map covered stretching studies in healthy athletes. Six databases were searched to 1 January 2023 under PRISMA-ScR, and 300 trials involving 7,080 athletes across 43 sports were included. Most trials studied acute effects of static active stretching or dynamic stretching in the warm-up, with outcomes mostly limited to general performance tests.
paper.tldr: Stretching research in healthy athletes is narrow: mostly acute warm-up studies of static and dynamic stretching in male athletes, with chronic, dose-response, sport-specific and injury outcomes largely unexplored. Five injury trials exist and none supported a preventive effect.
paper.methods: Systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map following PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-ScR and Cochrane guidance. Six databases were searched, three authors independently screened records with a fourth arbitrating, and data were extracted within participant, intervention, comparator, outcome, study design and context domains, then synthesized narratively with descriptive counts.
paper.findings: 300 trials (316 publications) with 7,080 athletes were included, mostly tier 2 and 3 athletes; 65.3% of athletes were male and 20.6% female. Static active stretching appeared in 62.3% of trials and dynamic stretching in 38.3%, with 85% of trials applying stretching within the warm-up. Chronic interventions averaged 7.4 weeks and never exceeded 6 months, and only five trials assessed injury outcomes.
paper.limitations: The review does not estimate effect sizes, and no risk-of-bias assessment is described. Most trials were underpowered (94% had fewer than 51 athletes), reporting of dose and intensity was inconsistent, and 66% of trials gave no funding statement. Percentages are not on a single denominator: the Results tier and sport percentages (for example 18 tier 4 trials, 4.8%) appear to use a denominator of about 374, while the Discussion's 22 tier 4 trials (7.3%) adds the mixed tier 3 and 4 trials over 300.
paper.practicalImplications: The best-studied case is acute static or dynamic stretching of the lower limbs in the warm-up of adult male, non-elite athletes compared with passive controls. Staff should not transfer these results to female, youth, elite or extreme-range-of-motion athletes, to long-term use, or to post-exercise stretching, which the review found little evidence for.
paper.athleteDev: Use this review to see where stretching evidence is thin before changing a warm-up or training block. Most trials measured general tests such as strength, power, range of motion and sprint after acute stretching, so the review does not show gains in sport-specific performance.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It excluded injured athletes and rehabilitation studies, so it says nothing about stretching for recovery from injury, and its authors limit their conclusions to healthy athletes at tier 2 or higher.

records.sourceFile: Where does blood flow restriction fit in the Toolbox of athletic development - A narrative review of the proposed mechanisms and potential applications.pdf

paper.citation: Davids CJ, Roberts LA, Bjørnsen T, Peake JM, Coombes JS, Raastad T. Where Does Blood Flow Restriction Fit in the Toolbox of Athletic Development? A Narrative Review of the Proposed Mechanisms and Potential Applications. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: Blood flow-restricted exercise is used as a low-intensity, time-efficient approach to gain many of the benefits of typical high-intensity training. This narrative review evaluates BFR as an additional training method for athletes, outlines its proposed mechanisms of action, and proposes how practitioners can use it alongside high-load training.
paper.tldr: Blood flow restriction is a useful add-on for athletes, mainly for muscle size and local endurance, but it does not replace heavy training for maximal strength and power. Introduce it gradually to limit excessive muscle stress.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on BFR in athletes and trained individuals, with mechanistic and applied sections and a practical table of recommendations. The text does not describe a systematic search.
paper.findings: Low-load BFR resistance training increased muscle size at a magnitude similar to high-load training, including in trained athletes, while strength gains were usually smaller. Conventional BFR had little effect on jump or sprint performance. High-frequency BFR blocks (five or more sessions per week) produced large increases in satellite cell numbers and myonuclei in cited studies, alongside transient fatigue and strength loss. Combined BFR and endurance work improved aerobic capacity and local endurance in cited studies.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no described search. Many cited athlete studies are small, some hypertrophy outcomes rely on girth or other proxies, and several mechanistic findings come from untrained individuals. The authors note that separate-session or block BFR has not been investigated in athletic cohorts and that hypertrophy responses to same-session BFR are unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Use BFR as a supplement to high-load training, not a replacement. Screen athletes first and introduce high-frequency blocks gradually, which the authors suggest early in pre-season and not close to competition.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: BFR can be added to strength and endurance blocks to build muscle size and local endurance at low loads, and high-frequency blocks may suit pre-season. Conventional low-load BFR does not appear to improve power or sprint performance, although some studies combining BFR with sprint or high-load work report gains, so keep high-load work in the programme.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review describes a four-step model from Loenneke et al. (BFR alone or with NMES or isometric work during immobilisation, then walking or cycling with BFR, low-load BFR resistance exercise, and finally high-load training) based mainly on rehabilitation studies. It does not test return-to-play criteria and should not be used as a validated return-to-sport protocol.

records.sourceFile: Why should athletes brake fast - Influence of eccentric velocity on concentric performance during countermovement jumps at different loads.pdf

paper.citation: Hernández-Davó JL, Sabido R, Omar-García M, Boullosa D. Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Influence of Eccentric Velocity on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps at Different Loads. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: The study compared four eccentric tempos (5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated) on eccentric kinetics and kinematics and on the concentric performance of loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM in 13 well-trained participants.
paper.tldr: In this single session, faster eccentric phases in loaded jumps increased end-eccentric work and jump velocity compared with slower tempos. Treat this as a reason to trial fast eccentrics and monitor the result, not as a settled training rule.
paper.methods: Randomised, within-participant repeated-measures design. Thirteen well-trained young men completed 12 sets (four eccentric tempos by three loads) of four loaded countermovement jumps after 1RM testing and two familiarisation sessions. Barbell kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a linear position transducer, and a two-way MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests was used.
paper.findings: The accelerated tempo produced greater total eccentric work than all other tempos at each load. Eccentric work in the last 100 ms was greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s and 2 s tempos at each load. Early concentric force, peak velocity and mean propulsive velocity were greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s and 2 s tempos, with no differences between fast and accelerated. Eccentric depth did not differ by tempo or load. The change in end-eccentric work from the 5 s to the accelerated condition correlated strongly with the change in early concentric force (r = .774 to .880).
paper.limitations: This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, with no training outcome. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps without rest, unlike the other tempos, which confounds tempo with rest structure. The methods text refers once to a squat jump exercise, while the title, abstract and most of the text describe countermovement jumps.
paper.practicalImplications: In this session, a fast or continuous eccentric phase in loaded jumps gave more end-eccentric work and higher jump velocity than slower tempos. Whether this improves strength or power over a training block is not tested here, so trial it and monitor it rather than adopt it as a fixed rule.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Faster eccentric phases (fast or accelerated) raised end-eccentric work and jump velocity in well-trained men within one session. Coaches could trial fast eccentrics in loaded jumps, but the chronic effect on strength and power was not measured.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Not applicable. The study used healthy trained men and excluded those with joint injury in the prior 12 months, so it does not inform rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Why sports should embrace bilateral asymmetry - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Afonso J, Peña J, Sá M, Virgile A, García-de-Alcaraz A, Bishop C. Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review. Symmetry. 2022;14:1993.
paper.abstract: The paper critically reviews the evidence on the occurrence of bilateral asymmetry in sport and its effects on sports performance, injury risk and training, and it argues against assumptions that asymmetry is harmful.
paper.tldr: Bilateral asymmetry is common in sport, and there is no direct evidence that it impairs performance or causes injury. Asymmetry scores fluctuate a lot, so judge them against test error over repeated tests rather than from a single result.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on bilateral asymmetry in sport, organised around occurrence and performance, injury, and training effects. The text does not describe a systematic search.
paper.findings: Asymmetry is prevalent across several sports regardless of age, sex or competitive level, and can appear even in apparently symmetric actions such as running and rowing. Asymmetry measures are task-, metric- and sport-specific, fluctuate in size and direction over time, and correlate poorly with each other and with performance. Injuries tend to accentuate asymmetry; one prospective youth study found a small association with single-leg jump asymmetry and a systematic review found low to moderate evidence of association, but no study showed causation. Training programmes can reduce some asymmetries, but the review finds no evidence that this improves sport-specific performance or reduces injury risk.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no described search, so study selection is not reproducible. Sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, and much of the cited evidence is cross-sectional or based on standardized tests. The conclusion that asymmetry is not harmful relies partly on absence of evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not treat one asymmetry score as a problem to correct. Because asymmetry fluctuates and group means hide large individual variation, judge each athlete's scores against the test's typical error across repeated sessions, and do not assume that reducing asymmetry improves performance or lowers injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Asymmetry is common in athletes and the review argues against targeting symmetry for its own sake. Track interlimb differences across repeated tests, ignore changes within test error, and judge them against performance outcomes rather than a fixed symmetry target.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review accepts reducing large injury-related asymmetries during rehabilitation but questions fixed, arbitrary symmetry thresholds, and notes that limb symmetry indices can mislead when both limbs remain below pre-injury capacity. It does not test any clearance criteria, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Workload and injury in professional soccer players - Role of injury tissue type and injury severity.pdf

paper.citation: Enright K, Green M, Hay G, Malone JJ. Workload and Injury in Professional Soccer Players: Role of Injury Tissue Type and Injury Severity. Int J Sports Med. 2020;41:89-97.
paper.abstract: Twenty-eight days of GPS training data before 264 non-contact injuries from 192 professional soccer players were examined. After exclusions, 124 injuries were compared by tissue type, and workload was related to days missed.
paper.tldr: Distance-based GPS workload measures, whether weekly totals or ACWR, did not distinguish muscle, tendon or ligament injuries, and showed little relation to days missed. Use them for general load monitoring, not as a tissue-specific injury signal.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of 28 days of pre-injury Catapult GPS data (total distance, high-speed distance and sprint distance) from eight clubs. Injuries were classified by tissue type using ultrasound confirmation and by days missed. Accumulated 1 to 4 week loads and ACWRs were compared across tissue types with one-way ANOVA and correlated with severity.
paper.findings: No significant differences in any accumulated weekly load or ACWR method between muscle, tendon and ligament injuries (P > 0.05). The text reports no significant correlation between any workload variable and injury severity (P > 0.05), but Table 3 shows one correlation at P = 0.038 (2-week accumulated sprint distance, r = -0.186). Muscle injuries were the largest group (n = 79).
paper.limitations: 140 of 264 injuries (53 percent) were excluded for inconsistent or missing data. The Discussion says almost all of 142 injuries fell in the ACWR sweet-spot zone, which does not match the 124 injuries analysed. The text's null severity result conflicts with the Table 3 correlation at P = 0.038, and the 1-week sprint row prints r = -0.84, probably a typo for -0.084. The design is observational and uses a single set of distance variables.
paper.practicalImplications: Use weekly GPS totals and ACWR for overall load monitoring, but do not expect them to show which tissue a player is at risk of injuring or how long they will be out. Tissue-specific planning would need other load measures, such as jumping and landing, which this study could not capture.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Weekly distance totals and ACWR from this study do not distinguish injury types, so they should not be used alone to explain why an athlete was hurt. They remain useful as general training-load context.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not address return-to-play timing. Workload measures showed little relation to days missed, so they should not be used alone to predict how long an injured player will be out.

records.sourceFile: Workload monotony strain and non-contact injury incidence in professional football players.pdf

paper.citation: Delecroix B, Mccall A, Dawson B, Berthoin S, Dupont G. Workload monotony, strain and non-contact injury incidence in professional football players. Science and Medicine in Football. 2018.
paper.abstract: Season-long cohort of 130 elite players from five European teams, with internal workload from session-RPE. Poisson regression tested weekly, 2-week, 3-week and 4-week monotony and strain against non-contact injury incidence.
paper.tldr: In five European professional squads, a high 4-week workload strain was associated with more non-contact injuries and a high 4-week monotony with fewer. These are associations from one observational season, so use them alongside other factors rather than as injury thresholds.
paper.methods: Internal load was session-RPE multiplied by session or match duration for all training and matches. Monotony (mean divided by standard deviation) and strain (monotony multiplied by load) were calculated daily over rolling 1 to 4 week windows and related to injury incidence with Poisson regression.
paper.findings: 237 non-contact injuries, 7.4 per 1000 h, of which 58 were re-injuries that were counted in the total. 4-week monotony: RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.90; P = 0.004). 4-week strain: RR 1.50 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.97; P = 0.004). Monotony and strain over 1 to 3 weeks were not significantly associated with incidence.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the association does not establish causation and that staff who recorded the workload may have adapted sessions. session-RPE is subjective, and re-injuries are included in the 237 injuries analysed. The predictive value of the measures was not assessed. The Practical implications box says high monotony and strain are associated with an increase in injury incidence, which contradicts the Results (monotony RR 0.72) and Conclusion (regular workload protective); the Results are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Track 4-week strain (load multiplied by monotony) alongside other measures, and watch for sustained very high, very regular load across congested fixture periods. Also reduce large day-to-day swings between rest, training and match days, as the authors suggest. Do not use either measure as a stand-alone injury threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Sustained high strain across a month of congested fixtures is worth monitoring, since it was linked to more non-contact injuries. The study does not measure performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study covers injury incidence across squads, not return to play, so it cannot inform when an injured player is ready to come back.
